claim: Brain scans show that even tax-like, compulsory gifts to charity light up reward areas, and voluntary giving lights them up more.
evidence: even mandatory, tax-like transfers to a charity elicit neural activity in areas linked to reward processing
source: Harbaugh WT, Mayr U, Burghart DR. Neural responses to taxation and voluntary giving reveal motives for charitable donations. Science 316: 1622, 2007
author: Harbaugh, Mayr, Burghart
caveat: Small fMRI sample (19 students; DOI not yet resolved
column19: Reel: 'Your brain treats giving like getting'

claim: People who had spent money on others in the past month reported more wellbeing in 120 of 136 countries surveyed.
evidence: a positive relationship between personal well-being and spending on others in 120 of 136 countries
source: Aknin LB et al. Prosocial spending and well-being: cross-cultural evidence for a psychological universal. J Pers Soc Psychol 104(4), 2013 (APA press release)
author: Aknin et al.
caveat: Correlational (Gallup World Poll 2006-08). A 2020 registered replication found smaller effects for the experimental version: say 'linked to', not 'causes'.

claim: A Science paper argued that how you spend money may matter as much for happiness as how much you earn; spending on others beat spending on yourself.
evidence: we suggest that how people spend their money may be at least as important as how much money they earn
source: Dunn EW, Aknin LB, Norton MI. Spending money on others promotes happiness. Science 319(5870): 1687-1688, 2008
author: Dunn, Aknin, Norton
caveat: Experiment was small (46 people; DOI not yet resolved
verified_by: check); effect sizes in later replications were smaller. Pair with KH002 and say so.

claim: A 2024 BMJ review of randomised trials found walking or jogging, yoga and strength training all reduced depression, with walking/jogging among the strongest.
evidence: walking or jogging (n=1210, κ=51, Hedges’ g −0.62, 95% credible interval −0.80 to −0.45)
source: Noetel M et al. Effect of exercise for depression: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ 384: e075847, 2024
author: Noetel et al.
caveat: Not a replacement for treatment; say 'alongside', never 'instead of'. Many trials were low certainty.
use_in: Reel: 'A walk is in the depression guidelines now'

claim: Marcus told himself that when he wanted cheering up, he should think about the good qualities of the people around him.
evidence: When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee
author: Marcus Aurelius
caveat: Section number by convention; Standard Ebooks has no section numbers (book-level check).

claim: Marcus: when you've done someone a good turn, why look for a third thing, like credit or a favour back?
evidence: When thou hast done a good act and another has received it, why dost thou look for a third thing besides these
author: Marcus Aurelius

claim: Marcus thought real kindness can't be beaten, as long as it is genuine and not a performance.
evidence: a good disposition is invincible, if it be genuine, and not an affected smile and acting a part
author: Marcus Aurelius
caveat: The tracker's 16 Nov reel cites 11.18 with 'verify wording': this is Long's wording.

claim: An old Buddhist verse: hatred does not end by hatred, only by love.
evidence: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
source: The Dhammapada, Sacred Books of the East vol. X (Project Gutenberg #2017)
author: attributed to the Buddha
caveat: Müller's 1881 translation; modern ones say 'non-hatred' or 'love'.

claim: The Tao Te Ching compares the highest good to water: it helps everything and doesn't compete.
evidence: The highest excellence is like (that of) water.
author: Laozi (attributed)
caveat: Authorship of the Tao Te Ching is traditional, not certain.

claim: Knowing others is clever; knowing yourself is wiser.
evidence: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent.
author: Laozi (attributed)

claim: A student said he did not want to do to others what he wouldn't want done to him. Confucius told him he hadn't got there yet.
evidence: What I do not wish men to do to me, I also wish not to do to men." The Master said, "Ts'ze, you have not attained to that.
author: Confucius
caveat: The better-known version is Analects XV.23; it was beyond the part of the Gutenberg file we could read, so check it before using.
use_in: Reel: 'Confucius told his student: not yet'
